newsitem.title: USA: Mass. lawmakers mull tort reform for jobs.
newsitem.headline: Mass. lawmakers mull tort reform for jobs.

text.p: Legislation that spurs economic growth found its way to the Massachusetts Judiciary Committee Wednesday when a thinktank released a report showing tort reform would create more than 241,000 new jobs, State House News reported.

The report "Taxation by Litigation" released by the Beacon Hill Institute estimated that passing a bill reforming the state's tort system could create 241,244 new jobs in Massachusetts and the Judiciary Committee heard testimony on a measure backed by the institute.

"In this study, we found that tort suits are creating a chilling effect on the business community," said David Tuerck, executive director of the institute. "Everyone in this state is paying an indirect 'tort tax' because of this tort system, which is hurting our economy."
Tuerck and others said the threat of illegitimate lawsuits stunts job growth and thwarts expansion and leads to higher prices.
The report states that liability insurance has forced companies to increase the price of groceries by 3 percent, automobile repair by 5 percent, and step ladders by 30 percent.
The institute applauded a bill filed by Sen. Richard Moore, D-Uxbridge, that aims to lower the cost of torts for businesses.
* eliminates joint liability, making manufacturers liable for only the percentage of harm their product caused; * empowers judges to sanction attorneys who file frivolous lawsuits;

* enacts a 15-year "state of the art" defense, in which manufacturers could claim that their products were made with the most up-to-date technology available, and therefore could not be defective * forces plaintiffs under the influence of alcohol or drugs at the time of their injuries to prove that their impairment did not help cause the harm.
A similar law passed in Illinois in 1995 dropped tort filings there by 26.6 percent the next year, Tuerck said.
Using that figure, he said, Massachusetts would add 139,940 jobs, and increase state tax revenues by $314 million. A more significant drop in such lawsuits could create 241,224 new jobs, he said.
But Marilyn Beck, the president-elect of the Massachusetts Bar Association, said proponents exaggerate the losses. That includes the Weld administration, she said.

Reading from a 1996 letter from the National Center for State Courts, Beck said supporters have misrepresented figures that suggest Massachusetts has thousands of more tort cases filed than states like New Jersey, New York and California.
"In fact," Beck said at the hearing, "there has been a decline in Superior Court civil cases every year since 1990." That number has dropped by almost 33 percent, she said.
